title: Iran flatly rejects Trump's claim of 11-hour Oman negotiations — Gharibabadi says no US officials present
narrative: On Monday, July 14, 2026, President Donald Trump told Fox News chief foreign correspondent Trey Yingst that US negotiators believed they had reached a "long-term peace deal with Iran" following an 11-hour meeting on July 12. Trump said the meeting took place and that Iranian leaders later "introduced new demands" after the apparent breakthrough. The claim was presented as evidence that diplomacy was progressing despite the ongoing military campaign. On Tuesday, July 15, Iran's Deputy Foreign Minister for Legal and International Affairs Kazem Gharibabadi appeared on Iranian state television and categorically rejected the claim. "The claim that 11 hours of negotiations were held with the United States is not true and is strongly rejected," Gharibabadi said. He stated that Iran's discussions during its recent visit to Oman were limited to meetings with Omani officials only — there were no negotiations with the US side. Gharibabadi said Iran had proposed a new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz to Omani officials and had shown "maximum goodwill" in those discussions, but that no American negotiators were present. Separately, Gharibabadi addressed Trump's announcement that the United States would unilaterally declare itself the "Guardian of the Hormuz Strait" and demand a 20% reimbursement on all cargo passing through it. He said Iran would exercise "full sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, no matter the costs," including Oman's half, and that during wartime "Iran must control all of the Strait." He accused Washington of having "completely dismantled" the June 17 Islamabad memorandum of understanding through its reimposition of the naval blockade.
telemetry: Trump told Fox News on July 14 that US negotiators had an 11-hour meeting with Iranian officials on July 12 in Oman, claiming they reached a "long-term peace deal" before Iran "introduced new demands."

Iran's Deputy FM Gharibabadi on state television July 15: "The claim that 11 hours of negotiations were held with the United States is not true and is strongly rejected." He stated discussions were limited to Omani officials only — no US side present.
Gharibabadi said Iran proposed a new shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz to Omani officials and showed "maximum goodwill" in those discussions, but no American negotiators were present.
The Islamabad MOU signed June 17 established a 60-day ceasefire window. The US reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports on July 14, which Gharibabadi says "dismantled" the agreement.
Gharibabadi: Iran will exercise "full sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz, no matter the costs," including Oman's half, and during wartime "Iran must control all of the Strait."
CGTN (Chinese state media) rebroadcast Gharibabadi's denial — China signaling acceptance of Iran's version of events.
Vatican News reported "signs of strain" in the Oman talks. PBS headline: "Trump says Iran has requested a meeting, but Iranian officials say nothing has been scheduled."
Neither side has produced documentary evidence. Oman, the host country, has not issued a public statement clarifying whether US and Iranian officials were in the same room.
analysis: The factual contradiction is direct and on-record: Trump says 11 hours of US-Iran negotiations occurred on July 12 in Oman; Gharibabadi says zero negotiations with the US occurred. Both statements are from official, on-the-record sources. No third party has independently confirmed or denied which version is accurate. The asymmetry in verifiability is the load-bearing finding. Trump's claim describes a specific event — 11 hours, July 12, Oman — that should be confirmable through Omani diplomatic records, US State Department travel logs, or satellite imagery of delegations entering and leaving Muscat. Iran's denial is equally specific: discussions limited to Omani officials, no US side present. Neither side has produced documentary evidence. The Oman government's silence is itself a data point. If 11 hours of talks occurred on Omani soil, Muscat would have a diplomatic interest in confirming or denying. Their silence suggests either the talks did not happen as described, or Oman is being deliberately opaque about a process it considers sensitive. This mirrors the structural pattern of the June 17 G7 endorsement, where Trump declared a "very strong deal, nobody knows what it is" — a claimed agreement with no public text, no signatories, and contradictory characterizations from the two parties. The reimposition of the naval blockade on July 14 — the same day Trump claimed diplomatic progress — creates a physical contradiction alongside the verbal one: you do not reimpose a blockade against a party you are negotiating a long-term peace deal with. CGTN's amplification of Iran's denial adds a geopolitical layer: China is signaling it accepts Iran's version of events, which complicates any future US attempt to build a multilateral narrative around the Oman talks.
verdict: [SIPHONED VERDICT]: Trump claims 11 hours of US-Iran negotiations in Oman on July 12; Iran's Deputy FM categorically denies any US officials were present — the same day Trump reimposed the naval blockade, creating a physical contradiction with the claimed diplomatic progress.
